newsitem.title: USA: Industry sees slim list of choices for energy slot.
newsitem.headline: Industry sees slim list of choices for energy slot.

text.p: Conventional wisdom Thursday put Deputy Energy Secretary Charles Curtis and Democratic Rep. Bill Richardson of New Mexico at the top of the list of candidates to replace Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary.

Other names included Under Secretary of Energy Thomas Grumbly, Environmental Protection Agency administrator Carol Browner, former Deputy Energy Secretary Bill White, and retiring Sen. Bennett Johnston, a Louisiana Demcrat.
O'Leary had not officially resigned as of Thursday, but Energy Department officials confirmed Wednesday that she was stepping down.
Industry officials said Richardson and Curtis would both be well-suited to the job.

Coming from a state which produces oil and gas, has two major Energy Department research labs and a planned federal nuclear waste site, Richardson is knowledgeable on department issues. He was also a founding member of a renewable energy coalition in the House.
"He'd certainly be a good choice," said Dan Fager, a lobbyist for Chevron Corp.
If Clinton was looking to ensure that he included minorities in his Cabinet, Richardson, a Hispanic, would have an advantage.

"With two Hispanic Cabinet members leaving, there's going to be a real push to replace the diverse Cabinet (Clinton) has had," said Scott Denman, executive director of the Safe Energy Communications Council.
Richardson, who was just reelected to his eighth term in Congress, Thursday did not rule out interest in a cabinet position but said talk of an appointment was only speculation.
"I am very happy in my present job serving New Mexico's 3rd Congressional district," he said in a statement, declining to comment on whether he wanted to move to the administration.
If Clinton was looking for continuity, the obvious choices would be Curtis or Grumbly, who are both well-respected, with broad experience in energy issues.
"If it was offered, (Curtis) would take it," an Energy Department official said.
Browner has no energy experience, and an administration official said she had no plans to leave EPA.
Bill White, who left the Energy Department last year, is head of the Democratic Party in Texas, and recently formed a new company. He did not rule out a return to Washington.
"Right now I'm concentrating on the Texas Democrats winning the special elections," White said. "The truth is I'm not lobbying to do anything."
Industry officials considered Sen. Johnston a long-shot because he opposed the administration on nuclear waste policy, which makes up a large portion of the Energy Department portfolio.
If history repeats itself, none of the people named so far will get the job. Four years ago when Clinton was looking to fill the slot, O'Leary was never mentioned among the range of obvious choices.
